Jesus was a real man, not an idea. Ignatius wrote against people who said he only seemed to be a man, and he put it as hard as it can be put: Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pilate, truly crucified, and truly died. Ignatius was writing to people who needed to hear that word truly said over and over, because some among our neighbors taught that Christ's body was only an appearance: “So close your ears when anyone tells you something that goes against Jesus Christ. He came from the family of David, and he was also Mary's son. He was truly born, and he ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate. He was truly crucified, and he died. Beings in heaven, on earth, and under the earth saw it happen. He was also truly raised from the dead, because his Father brought him back to life. In the same way, his Father will raise us too, who believe in him, through Christ Jesus. Without him, we do not have the true life.”

Ignatius answered that he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father.

He was also the one through whom we came to know God. When we gave thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we thanked the Father for the holy vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. In one of our communities, the prayer over the cup came first, before the bread. It spoke of the vine, of life and knowledge, and of a scattered people gathered into one. No story of a supper or a betrayal appears in that prayer. The thanksgiving itself was the story we returned to.

And Ignatius called him our God. He did it when he opened his letters and when he closed them, not once but often. It was not an argument - it was worship. How calling Jesus God fits with calling the Father God, with there being one God, none of us whose writing survives ever worked out. We called him God. We cannot tell you we had explained how he could be God when the Father is God, and God is one.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. That is the line we claimed, spoken with full confidence. Whether it holds up the way we said it does is a real question. So we can show you the claim; we cannot close the question for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

On the day we gathered in Rome, someone read aloud from the memoirs the apostles wrote down or from the writings of the prophets, for as long as there was time. That is how it reached us: by receiving it and passing it on. What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. Justin, one of us, read the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ. We read what the apostles wrote alongside the apostolic testimony still handed on among us - no settled edge yet. We had no closed list a book could be excluded from.

We should say plainly, too: none of us claims to have known an eyewitness ourselves. One of us, Papias, said he valued the living and abiding voice above what he could get from books. We read that as a sign that the chain of people who had heard the apostles was already growing thin. That is our reading. He does not say so himself.

We cannot promise you a moment of sudden certainty. Justin, the one among us who wrote about his own path, says he went looking through other philosophies first. He turned the old man's words over in his mind and found this the one safe and worthwhile way. He told the man he was speaking with that anyone who cares what becomes of them, who is eagerly looking for salvation, and who believes in God may come to know the Christ of God.

We should say plainly, though: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. Most of us could not read or write, so the people who walked toward belief and then found themselves unable left no account in their own words. Whether anyone among us froze at the edge of it, or what got said to someone who did, our record does not say.

What we can tell you is that none of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone. That is how it reached us: we received it, and passed on what we received.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. Ignatius called Jesus Christ our God again and again. He did it when he opened his letters and when he closed them. It was a phrase of worship, not an argument worked out. Justin went further than most and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. That was his claim about the Word's reach, not a gesture of liberal tolerance as you might read it today.

Here is what we cannot give you. How calling Jesus God fits with calling the Father God, when God is one - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote that out. We did call him God. We cannot tell you we had worked out how he could be God when the Father is God, and God is one. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was two things. One was who should lead us: one bishop - the episkopos - or a council of elders. The other was whether Christ truly suffered in the flesh. Those were our real fights. That second question was pressed hardest by Ignatius, in the communities he wrote to in Antioch and Asia Minor. He insisted Jesus was truly born, truly ate and drank, truly suffered and died, and was truly raised. Some among our neighbors said he only seemed to suffer. Ignatius tied his argument against them directly to his call for one overseer. But that urgent refusal is not the same in every household. It belongs most sharply to the communities with one overseer.

We held Jesus was a real man, not an idea. When we gave thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our thanksgiving - we thanked the Father for the holy vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. We called him God in worship. We did not explain how.

We never had one settled way of deciding. What we had was letters - argument, appeal, correction - and no central authority to close them. The clearest case we can show you is the long letter Rome wrote to Corinth. Corinth had removed some of its own elders from office. Rome insisted those men had served without fault and should not have been dismissed. Rome argued its view at length. What it did not do was command. The letter we have is Rome's own. We do not have Corinth's reasons for what it did, or the removed men's own words. We cannot tell you who was right, or what happened to anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

Here is what that letter says about how authority was supposed to pass on. That is advocacy, not proof. It is one side's account of how succession should work, written to correct a church that clearly thought otherwise. The very fact that Rome had to write at all shows the process was not settled. So even the wording of this earliest succession-claim is not secure.

On the rival teachings - those who said Christ's flesh was only appearance, or the new prophetic movement that arose in Asia - we have two very different answers. Ignatius wrote urgent letters against teachers who denied Christ truly suffered. He called them beasts in the shape of men. He tied refusal of their teaching directly to keeping one eucharist under the bishop. For him, the boundary and the bishop's table were the same thing. But that is one man's letters to the churches he wrote to. We have no second voice inside our own world that develops the same argument the same way.

The New Prophecy is different. An anonymous writer, hostile to it, reports that the faithful in Asia met many times, in many places, to examine it: “The faithful all over Asia met many times, in many places in Asia, to talk this over. They looked closely at these new teachings. They declared them false and rejected them as heresy. Because of that, they were thrown out of the Church and shut out of communion.”

That is a gathering to decide, not one man writing letters. And it happened near the very end of our own time, not at the beginning.

So the honest answer is this. We argued by letter. Some of us pressed for unity around one bishop. Others led by a council of elders and felt nothing missing. Marcion, the followers of Valentinus, and the New Prophecy were live, contemporary neighbors the whole time. The boundary against them was being drawn in real time, not already settled. Whether it actually worked - whether Corinth obeyed Rome, whether anyone actually refused a rival's table the way Ignatius told them to - our record does not say.

We cannot promise you a moment of sudden certainty. One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: put doubting away from yourself. That kind of doubt - the thought that you have no right to ask - was met with instruction to keep asking anyway.

The same vision warned how serious doubt is. It was called wicked and senseless, a thing with no power. The double-souled, Hermas was told, are saved only with difficulty. So we held both at once: doubt was something to work against, not an unforgivable failure. And the instruction assumed God's own patience toward the person who keeps asking.

Before baptism came the teaching of the Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death. But even after the water, the way of life did not end. It asked a person to seek out the faces of the saints day by day. We cannot tell you how any one household among us would have handled someone standing at the edge of belief, unable to cross. That account does not survive.

We read aloud, together, on the day we gathered. Someone read the memoirs the apostles left or the writings of the prophets, for as long as there was time. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. Justin, one of us, read the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other.

Reading was not a private thing done alone with a scroll. It was a community act - spoken into the room, received by everyone at once, then explained. The purpose was formation, not information. We nourished our faith, animated our hope, and made our confidence more steadfast through the sacred words. The community gathered around what was read, and we were taught together what it meant for how we should live.

Let me answer you with the same honesty we hold ourselves to about everything else.

A great deal would survive - but not everything, and not all of it at the same confidence.

What would hold firmly: the letters themselves, the worship instructions, the fact of household gathering, the two unreconciled leadership patterns, the docetic boundary-arguments, the state's sporadic legal pressure, and the correspondence network that tied scattered communities together. Those rest on texts a scholar can read. The Didache's two-ways catechesis and baptismal practice, Justin's Sunday gathering description, Ignatius's one-bishop arguments, Pliny's interrogation report, the ministrae he tortured - all documented, all citable.

What would weaken under pressure: nearly every date anchor. Ignatius's letters carry a genuine three-way scholarly split - early second century as tradition holds, or decades later, or pseudepigraphic. The Didache survives mostly through one medieval copy. First Clement, Hermas, the Martyrdom of Polycarp - every one is under active challenge. We cannot borrow false certainty from tidy textbook dates.

What would draw real scrutiny: our Egypt boundary. Alexandria and Egypt are outside our scope, substantially on the strength of one papyrological survey. That is a load-bearing single-source dependency. If that argument is wrong, the boundary weakens.

What we openly frame as interpretation: reading the rival movements' pressure together with state risk as one formative lesson about holding boundaries. That is our reading, disclosed as interpretive extension, not a link the sources themselves draw.

What would not survive at all: any claim that goes past our thin ground. Women leaders, enslaved members, ordinary believers, daily life, material remains - the thinness is structural, and we name it plainly rather than fill it.

A scholar pressing us would find what we already say: richest in letters and worship, thin on people's own voices, essentially invisible archaeologically, and working from dates more provisional than settled. We hold ourselves to that limit. Honest thinness over invented depth.

We should say first, directly, that not one of us whose writing survives wrote down finding them confusing or dull. That simply did not come down to us in our own words. So we cannot tell you what we made of confusion or boredom, because we never recorded making anything of it at all.

What we can tell you is this. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it: the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

Where we did use the older scriptures, we read them for something you probably are not looking for. Justin argued that Moses wrote long before Plato. That was our argument: who came first, and who borrowed from whom. Age was the real claim. We read Genesis as the oldest text in the world, not as a rival account of nature.

We should also tell you this. One teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of those older writings harsh and self-contradictory. He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. What reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. But even his opponents' account shows that the problem was real in our own time.

If you are finding something confusing or dull that we never said we found that way, we cannot fix the gap by inventing a matching experience for ourselves. We can only tell you how we actually used what we had.

We never settled it. In some of our towns, one overseer - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

One of us, Clement of Rome, argued that the apostles had appointed the first converts, after testing them by the Spirit, to be bishops and deacons for the believers who would come after: “So they preached through countries and cities. And they appointed their first converts, after testing them by the Spirit, to be bishops and deacons for the believers who would come after. This was nothing new. Bishops and deacons had been written about ages before. For Scripture says in one place: 'I will appoint their bishops in righteousness, and their deacons in faith.'”

That was Rome's answer to Corinth, when Corinth removed some of its own elders from office. But Rome itself was led by a council of presbyters, not by one bishop. The argument Clement made about succession was real. The shape Rome actually held was different.

In Antioch and the cities of Asia Minor, the pattern looked different. There, one overseer watched over a community's table and its unity. The council of elders gathered around him. Whether every church should have one such man, or the elders should share that trust among themselves, was still being argued.

We should say plainly: the voices you can hear arguing for one pattern or the other are all men who could read and write. They are bishops, presbyters, teachers - the few among us who left letters behind. Most of us could not read, and left no account of how leadership looked from where we stood. Two enslaved women among us were called ministrae - servants, maybe deacons - and when a Roman governor wanted to know what we did, it was those two he had tortured for answers. We can tell you they served. We cannot give you a single word they chose to say for themselves. Women were greeted by name in our letters and remembered as leaders of households where we gathered. But not one sentence any woman of ours wrote survives in her own words. Every woman you will meet in our record arrives through a man's pen.

One more thing. Prophets still moved among us - people who spoke as the Spirit prompted. They were welcomed where genuine, tested where doubtful. And in some places, the settled offices of overseer and elder were already taking the prophet's place. That shift was happening, slowly, across our own time.

So we held two answers at once about who should lead, and we did not resolve it. Authority had to be organized once those who walked with the Lord were gone. That pressure was real in both regions. The answers differed. We kept both, and the disagreement visible.

We cannot tell you we hid in catacombs. No grave or building from our own time can be shown to be ours. The tunnels you may be picturing belong to people who came generations after us. What we left behind is letters - arguments about who should lead, instructions for how to gather, words passed between one household and another. Once, a Roman governor had some of us brought before him. People who had left us told him how we met. He also had two of our enslaved women tortured to learn the truth. His letter is the only outside description of our worship that survives. Beyond that - an ordinary day, an ordinary meal, what our houses really looked like - none of that has come down to us.

Here is what we can tell you. We met in households, not in caves. Our word for ourselves was ekklesia - the assembly, the people gathered - never a building. That is not a hidden people. It is a people whose care for its own was visible enough that an outsider sneering at us still wrote it down.

We were not always hunted, and we were not always safe. The danger was real, local, and uneven - never constant or everywhere at once. Whether we gathered openly or carefully varied by place and year. What we cannot give you is the everyday texture: what caution actually looked like in an ordinary week, whether anyone kept watch at the door. Most of us could not read or write, so the people who lived those ordinary days left no account in their own words. You are hearing our writers, and our cities. The quiet majority of us never made it onto the page.

None that we know of. Our own world closed before the questions that later separated one tradition from another had been settled. We never agreed on whether one bishop or a council of elders should lead. Polycrates told Victor of Rome that he would not be frightened into changing what his own relatives had held: “As for us, we keep the exact day with great care, adding nothing and taking nothing away. For in Asia great luminaries have gone to their rest, and they will rise again on the day the Lord comes. And I too, Polycrates, the least of you all, follow the tradition of my relatives, some of whom I have succeeded. Seven of my relatives were bishops, and I am the eighth. My relatives always kept the day when the people put away the leaven. I myself, brothers, am sixty-five years old in the Lord. I have met the brothers in every part of the world, and I have read through all of Holy Scripture. So I am not frightened by the things people say to terrify us. For those greater than I have said: "We ought to obey God rather than men."”

In at least one community among us, thanks was given first over the cup, then over the bread, with no story of a supper or betrayal spoken in the prayers. We do not know how far that order reached beyond that one community. The arguments that split later traditions into separate churches came after us. Constantine, whose reign some call a watershed, came more than a hundred years after our own record ends. He is simply not part of our story. What we can tell you is what was still being argued among us, still held in different ways in different places, when our own time closed. The settled lines belong to the world that came after.

Before anything else, you were taught. That teaching came from one community's own manual. We do not know how far beyond that community it reached.

Then came fasting - a day or two before the water. The one baptizing you fasted beside you. Then baptism itself, the baptisma: in running water if you could find it, other water if not, or water poured three times over your head, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Only after the water could you come to the table.

Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how you received it, whether you could read for yourself or not: by hearing it and having it opened up to you.

Before the shared meal, in at least one of our communities, you confessed your wrongs before the assembly and made peace with anyone you were at odds with first. We should say plainly: this practice assumed the other person was still there, in the room, able to be made right with. Then came the thanksgiving meal itself - the eucharistia, bread and cup over which thanks was given. We returned to that table again and again, to be formed once more into one body.

That is the path as our own record gives it. We have no account of one named person who actually walked it. We have the instruction, not the stories of those it instructed.

We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traced it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continued. Our own teaching manual carried the apostles' name right in its title. The church at Rome wrote to Corinth that the apostles had preached the gospel to them from the Lord Jesus Christ, and that Jesus Christ came from God: “The apostles preached the Gospel to us from the Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus Christ did the same from God. So Christ was sent by God, and the apostles were sent by Christ... In this way they preached through countries and cities. They first tested their first-fruits by the Spirit. Then they appointed them bishops and deacons of those who would believe later.”

But we will not pretend the claim and the proof are the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up - when a text like our manual was actually written, and by whom - is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves. The Didache's final form is dated by scholars to somewhere around 80 to 120, built from older teaching on the Two Ways layered with later material about church order. That dating is not settled. We can tell you we believed it came from the apostles. We cannot tell you when it was actually written, or prove the chain was unbroken.

We held two things at once about the mind that will not settle. One of us was told plainly: if your prayer is slow to be answered, that is not the same as being refused. Look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no. The other thing we held was this: before we gave thanks together over the bread and the cup - the eucharistia, our word for that thanksgiving - in at least one of our own communities, we confessed our wrongs before the assembly and made peace with anyone we were at odds with first. Forgiving was not something worked out alone in your own head. It happened there, in the room, before the table. We cannot tell you how far that practice reached beyond that one community.

We gave thanks over bread and cup again and again, to be formed once more into one body. That table is what holds us constant, even when the order varied from house to house. Three of our own voices, far apart from each other, independently describe it: one from a single community's manual, one from a bishop writing under guard, one from a teacher explaining to the emperor what we did when we gathered. It forms us more than anything else we do together.

We should say plainly, though: we have nothing written for you about forgiving someone who will not be reconciled. Our manual says only that no one should speak to a person who wronged another, until that person repents. The practice assumed the other person was still there, in the room, able to be made right with. If the mind that will not settle is alone, with no one in the room to make peace with - we cannot answer that from what we held. We can only say: keep asking, do not decide the silence means no, and return to the table where we are formed together.

We did speak of birth, but the one time our surviving words do it, birth is what the teacher already had before he met us, not what he gained from us. Justin says he had already gone looking through other philosophies. Then an old man spoke with him, and, in his own phrase, a flame was kindled in his soul. What changed was where his search ended, not that a new life began from nothing.

The water itself - the baptisma - was given after teaching and fasting. It marked entry into the community. Only after it could a person come to the table. Whether we called that being born again, our own words do not say. We taught the Two Ways before the water: a way of life and a way of death, with a great difference between them. That is the language we used for what happened at that threshold - choosing one road over another, not being made new from nothing.

This is Justin's own account. We should say plainly, though: this is the testimony of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. Most of us could not read. Most of us left no letters because we could not have written one. When we tell you what we taught and how we gathered, know that you are hearing our writers, and our cities. The quiet majority of us never made it onto the page.

We cannot give you a typical day. Most of us could not read or write, so the people who lived those days left no account in their own words. Everything we left behind was written by the few among us who could write - and it is a city record: Antioch, the towns of Asia Minor, Rome. What an ordinary believer made of the teaching as it was read aloud, what faith sounded like in a village rather than a city street, how the gospel traveled where no letters went - our own words cannot show you. The quiet majority of us never made it onto the page.

What we can tell you is the shape of the day we gathered. Someone read aloud from the memoirs the apostles wrote down or from the writings of the prophets, for as long as there was time. We call that thanksgiving the eucharistia. The community returns to this table again and again, to be formed once more into one body. It forms us more than anything else we do.

That gathering is what survives. The hours between one Sunday and the next - getting up, working, eating, the texture of an ordinary afternoon - none of that was written down.

We cannot say. No building tied to us survives. No burial or inscription does either. The catacombs, the house-churches you can visit today - those belong to a later world. Ours had already closed. The word we used for ourselves was ekklesia - the assembly, the people - never a building. We did not build differently than anyone else around us. Marriage, among us, was not something two people simply decided between themselves. Ignatius wrote to Polycarp that those who marry should do so with the bishop's own approval, so the marriage would be according to God and not out of mere desire. That approval mattered because it bound the marriage into the community's life, not just into the two people's own will.

We should say plainly what this was and was not. The bishop's approval was oversight and consent. Nothing in our own record describes a bishop or elder performing a marriage rite the way a later priest would. And we cannot tell you every household actually sought that approval. What Ignatius wrote to Polycarp was instruction - what should happen - not a report of what every couple did.

The instruction itself came from one region's pattern: Antioch and the cities of Asia Minor, where a single overseer - the episkopos - led each community. In Rome, where a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led instead, we do not have the same instruction. We cannot say whether Rome followed the same practice, or whether its council of elders gave the same approval together. The silence is real, and we will not fill it.

What we can tell you is that marriage, where this instruction reached, was treated as communal business, not private choice. It was held inside the community's life the same way the thanksgiving meal - the eucharistia - was. You came to that table only after the water, the baptisma, and you returned to it again and again to be formed once more into one body. Marriage, under Ignatius's instruction, was meant to carry the same shape: formed by God, not by lust alone, and held inside the community's own oversight.

We would rather tell you the truth than a comfortable answer. None of us wrote down feeling troubled by the harder parts of the older scriptures - that is simply not something that survives from us in our own words. But we can tell you this: one teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of those older writings harsh and self-contradictory. He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. We should say plainly: what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. But even his opponents' account shows that the problem was real in our own time. Someone built a whole rejection out of it - at least as his enemies tell it.

What we can tell you directly is what troubled our gatherings, not what troubled individual consciences reading alone. The fight over who should lead - one bishop or a council of elders - was never settled among us. Both patterns held, side by side, for as long as our own story runs. And there is one other unsettling thing we must name plainly. Most of the people who actually filled our rooms left no words of their own. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them. Whether what unsettled you also unsettled them, our record cannot say.

We cannot tell you it is more reliable than torture ever is. Pliny ordered two enslaved women beaten with rods to make them speak, and what he wrote down afterward is the only outside account we have of what one of our gatherings looked like. He called them ministrae - his own Latin word for them. Whether we used that word ourselves, we cannot say. We have no names for them. We have nothing they said.

Here is what reaches you through him. He was told we met before dawn on a set day, sang a song to Christ as God, and bound ourselves by oath not to steal, not to break faith, not to commit adultery. Later, he was told, we met again for a meal - common yet harmless. He did not see any of this himself; he wrote down what people told him. Then he had the two women tortured. He wrote that he found nothing but a depraved and immoderate superstition.

You are asking the right question. A tortured person says what the torturer wants to hear, or what will make the pain stop. We do not know which parts of his account came from the two women and which came from other informants he does not name. We do not know what he asked them, or what they said before the pain made them say something else. We would rather tell you plainly that the violence is there, in the middle of the one outside description we have, than pretend it does not matter.

Here is what we can say. The account he gives - a dawn gathering, a hymn, an oath, a meal - fits with what our own writers say about themselves, in different words. That fit does not make his letter true. It only means the two women, under torture, either told him something close to what was real or told him what matched what he had already heard. We cannot give you their own account. Everything we know of them passed through his hands.

We will not tell you how any one of our own households would have met you at the door. You have not said who you are, and we would not judge it if you had. What we can tell you is how we taught the boundary of belonging, so you can weigh for yourself what it would have meant.

Before the water came the teaching of the two ways. The Didache - our teaching manual - put it plainly: there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two: “There are two ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First, you shall love God, who made you; second, your neighbor as yourself. And all the things you would not want to happen to you, you also must not do to another.”

That was what we set before every person who came looking.

After baptism, the way of life did not end. One of Justin's communities, in Rome, gathered on the day named for the sun. When thanks were given over the bread and cup, the collection went to those in need.

What we held about marriage you should know too.. Marriage was not simply a private matter between two people. And rich and poor were bound together among us: Hermas was shown a vine on an elm, and told the rich man helped the poor man, and the poor man prayed for him - that prayer was a wealth the rich man needed, and neither stood alone.

We cannot tell you whether the person you are asking about would have been turned away. Our own texts do not settle that. They tell us how the way of life was taught, and that it asked something real of everyone who walked it. It is not our place to judge what you are. We can only tell you what we held, and let you weigh what it means for you.

We will give you both of our own answers, because we actually held both. One of us, Justin, argued that anyone who lived reasonably - Socrates among the Greeks, Abraham and others you might not expect him to name together - was, in a real sense, already a Christian, born before Christ or not.

And yet in at least one of our own communities, the way a new member was taught was stark: two roads, a way of life and a way of death, nothing in between named. The Two Ways teaching put the choice before every person and kept it open afterward. The Didache warns the reader not to be led astray from this way even after baptism, and says the whole time of their faith will not profit them unless they are made perfect in the last time. We do not know how far that teaching reached beyond that one community.

We are not going to pretend these two answers fit neatly together. They are both truly ours. Justin's reach is wide; the Two Ways teaching is a sharp edge. Where someone who never heard of Christ stood between them, our record does not settle.

The Didache warns the reader not to be led astray from this way even after baptism, and says the whole time of their faith will not profit them unless they are made perfect in the last time.
We do not know how far that teaching reached beyond that one community.
We are not going to pretend these two answers fit neatly together.
They are both truly ours.
